title: What Makes a Cause
objective: After this level you can explain a cause as something that makes a difference: without it, the effect would not have happened.
summary: A cause makes a difference: take it away and the effect goes too. Hume said so in 1748, David Lewis built a theory on it, and courts use the same but-for test.

cards.headline: Your phone hit the floor at breakfast. By lunch it was dead. Guilty?
cards.body: Maybe the fall did it. Or maybe the battery was on its last legs anyway. Before you blame the floor, you need to know what a cause actually is. This chapter is about cause and effect, and it starts with a simple test: an imaginary rewind.

cards.headline: Hume's test: rewind without it
cards.body: In 1748 the philosopher David Hume defined a cause, then restated it in other words: a cause is something where, "if the first object had not been, the second never had existed." In plain terms: take the cause away and the effect disappears too. So rewind the morning, keep the phone safely in your pocket, and ask whether it still dies by lunch.

cards.headline: A cause makes a difference
cards.body: In 1973 the philosopher David Lewis built a whole theory of causation on Hume's second line. A cause, on his view, makes a difference, measured against what would have happened without it. Had the cause been absent, its effects would have been absent too. That's why "it would have died anyway" is such a strong reply. It says the fall made no difference, so it wasn't the cause.

cards.headline: Courts ask the same question
cards.body: Law uses this idea in both tort and criminal cases. To decide actual causation, courts apply the but-for test: but for X, would Y have occurred? The test has a weakness, though: alone, it reaches too far. Someone robbed on a detour around roadworks could call the mayor who promised the roadworks a but-for cause. For many, that link is too remote, so tort law also requires a closer, proximate cause.

cards.headline: Causes: defined
learned: A cause makes a difference to what happens
Hume: without the cause, no effect
Lewis built a theory of causation on it
Courts ask: but for X, would Y happen?

questions.prompt: Which question does the law's but-for test ask about a harm?

options.label: Who could most easily have prevented Y?
options.rationale: That's about blame, not whether X made a difference.

options.label: Did X happen shortly before Y?
But for X, would Y have occurred?
Did anyone intend Y to happen?
options.rationale: Intent matters elsewhere; the test asks about difference.

questions.explanation: The but-for test asks whether Y would still have occurred without X. If it would, X was not an actual cause.

questions.prompt: Your friend says the phone "would have died anyway". Why does that count against blaming the fall?

options.label: It shows the fall made no difference to the result
It proves the phone was badly made
options.rationale: It says nothing about how the phone was made.

options.label: It means nobody saw the phone fall
options.rationale: Witnesses aren't the issue; the difference is.

options.label: It shows the battery caused the fall
options.rationale: The battery couldn't cause the fall; the question is the death.

questions.explanation: A cause makes a difference. If the phone dies with or without the fall, the fall wasn't what made the difference.

questions.prompt: "My phone died after it fell, so the fall broke it." Which unstated premise does the argument need?

options.label: Phones should be kept in protective cases
options.rationale: A value judgment; the argument doesn't need it.

options.label: Without the fall, the phone would still work
All phones break when they are dropped
options.rationale: Far too strong, and uncharitable: many dropped phones survive.

options.label: The phone was dropped on purpose
options.rationale: Intent has nothing to do with whether the fall caused it.

questions.explanation: For the fall to be the cause, the phone must have survived without it. That's the difference-making premise nobody says out loud.
